title: Lessons 1–2 · A Quiet Saturday
body:
It was Saturday.
I never set an alarm on Saturdays.
I usually stay in bed until ten.
Last Saturday I woke up very early.
Someone was talking loudly in the flat above me.
My neighbour was streaming a video game online.
He was shouting at his teammates all the time.
I got very angry.
I could not go back to sleep.

I knocked on the ceiling.
He did not pay any attention.
In the end, I could not bear it.
I sent him a message.
"I can't sleep!" I wrote.
"Sorry, I'm live right now," he replied.
"My viewers can hear you too!"
So I stayed in bed and watched short videos for hours.

Just then, my phone rang.
It was my sister, Amy.
"I've just arrived at the station," she said.
"I'm coming to see you."
"But I'm still lying in bed," I said.
"What are you doing?" she asked.
"I'm lying in bed," I repeated.
"Dear me," she said.
"Do you always get up so late?
It's half past twelve!"

"Dear me," she said.
"Do you always get up so late?
It's half past twelve!"

title: Lessons 3–4 · Posts From Abroad
body:
Social media always spoils my holidays.
Last summer, I went to Spain.
I visited old churches and sat in quiet squares.
A friendly guide taught me a few words of Spanish.
Then she sent me a list of good restaurants.
I took hundreds of photos on my phone.
Every evening I thought about my followers.
My holiday passed quickly, but I did not post a single photo.

My brother, Tim, is very different.
He is in Canada now.
He has been there for six months.
Tim is a software engineer.
He is working for a big company in Toronto.
He has already visited a great number of places.
He posts photos every day, and he sends me messages every week.
He has just bought a second-hand car.
Next month he will drive to the Rocky Mountains.
From there, he will fly to Vancouver.
Tim has never been abroad before, so he is finding everything very exciting.

Yesterday he sent me another message.
"Please send me a photo of you," he wrote.
"I haven't seen your face for months!"

title: Lessons 5–6 · The Drone and the Visitor
body:
I have just moved to a small village called Hillbury.
There is a bakery in the village.
It belongs to a woman called Anna Gray.
Anna has a shop in Hillbury, and she has just opened another shop in Oakfield.
Oakfield is only five miles from Hillbury, but there is no phone signal there.
So Anna has just bought a drone.
Yesterday, the drone carried the first message from one shop to the other.
It covered the distance in four minutes.
Up to now, Anna has sent a great many orders for bread, milk and eggs.
In this way, she has started her own private "internet".

Last night, a young man knocked at my door.
He asked me for a cup of tea and the Wi-Fi password.
In return for this, he fixed an old printer for me and played the guitar.
I gave him a cup of tea.
He drank the tea and connected his phone to my Wi-Fi.
Then he put a biscuit in his pocket and went away.
Later, a neighbour told me about him.
Everybody knows him.
His name is Leo Bell.
He calls at every house in the village once a month.
He always asks for a cup of tea and the Wi-Fi password.

title: Lessons 7–8 · Surprises at the Office
body:
The van was late, and the security guards were waiting at our office all morning.
They were expecting a valuable box of new phones from the factory.
A few hours earlier, someone had told the manager that thieves would try to steal the phones.
When the van arrived, some of the guards were waiting in the lobby while others were waiting in the car park.
Two men took the box out of the van and carried it into the meeting room.
While two guards were standing at the door, the manager opened the box.
To their surprise, the precious box was full of potatoes!

Our office is famous for something else too.
Every month we have a step challenge.
Nearly everybody enters it, but Joe Sanders wins every time.
Joe is the fittest person in our office.
Bill Frith is younger than Joe, and he runs faster than Joe.
But Joe takes more steps than anyone else.
He takes the stairs to the tenth floor every morning.
He has joined a hiking club and has walked across the whole city.
I like walking too, but I do not like hard work.
Every month I enter the challenge too, and I always win a little prize for the fewest steps in the office!

title: Lessons 9–10 · A New Year Party
body:
On Friday evening, we had a party at home.
It was the last day of the year.
A large group of friends had gathered in our living room.
We were watching the countdown on a big TV.
The clock on the screen would reach midnight in twenty minutes' time.
Fifteen minutes passed, and then, at five to twelve, the screen froze.
The numbers did not move.
We waited and waited, but nothing happened.
The Wi-Fi had stopped working!
Suddenly someone shouted, "It's two minutes past twelve!"
I looked at my phone.
It was true.
The internet refused to welcome the New Year.
At that moment, everybody began to laugh and sing.

We have an old record player in that room.
It was made in Japan in nineteen seventy-two.
It is kept on a shelf by the window.
It has belonged to our family for a long time.
It was bought by my grandfather many years ago.
That night, it was damaged by a visitor.
She wanted to play dance music from her phone.
She tried to connect her phone to it!
She pressed the buttons too hard, and the needle was broken.
My father was shocked.
Now we are not allowed to touch it.
It is being repaired by a friend of my father's.

title: 2026-11-04 · Why Most Experts Lose to a Boring Fund
body:
Every year, thousands of fund managers try to beat the market. They are smart, they work long hours, and they have more information than you do. Yet most of them fail.

The numbers are clear. Over fifteen years, about nine out of ten active funds in the United States do worse than a simple index fund. The results vary from year to year. In a good year, many managers do well. But very few can do it again and again.

Why? One reason is cost. An active fund charges a fee every year, often one percent or more. That does not sound substantial, but over thirty years it can eat a large part of your money. An index fund costs much less, so more of the return stays with you.

Another reason is that the market is efficient. When news comes out, millions of people react within seconds, and prices change before most of us can do anything. To beat the market, being smart is not sufficient. You have to be smarter than everyone else, and you have to be right before they are.

Nobody can predict the outcome of a single year. Even the experts cannot, and the honest ones admit it.

So what can an ordinary investor rely on? Time. If you buy a low-cost fund and keep adding money, your wealth grows gradually, almost without you noticing. It is boring, and that is exactly why it works.
